# Judges Chapter 11 — Disagreement Log
**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Date:** 2026-03-09

---

### v.3 — "worthless fellows" vs. "rough adventurers"

| Translator | Rendering | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| EMET | "worthless men" | anashim reqim — "empty men" |
| LOGOS | "worthless fellows" | Same |
| PNEUMA | "a band of rough adventurers" | Positive spin on reqim |

**SOPHIA's resolution:** Adopted LOGOS. The Hebrew reqim means "empty/worthless" — the same word used of Abimelech's followers in 9:4. PNEUMA's "rough adventurers" romanticizes what the text condemns. The narrator's word choice is deliberate: Jephthah's followers are the same caliber as Abimelech's mercenaries.

**Status:** Minor. Characterization — PNEUMA softens a negative term.

---

### v.29 — "the Spirit of the LORD was upon Jephthah" vs. "the Spirit of the LORD came upon Jephthah"

| Translator | Rendering | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| EMET | "the Spirit of YHWH was upon Yiphtach" | vattehi al-Yiphtach ruach YHWH |
| LOGOS | "the Spirit of the LORD was upon Jephthah" | Same — hayah al = "was upon" |
| PNEUMA | "the Spirit of the LORD came upon Jephthah" | "Came upon" for "was upon" |

**SOPHIA's resolution:** Adopted LOGOS. Consistent with the resolution in 3:10 (Othniel). The Hebrew vattehi al uses hayah ("to be") + al ("upon"), describing a state, not an event. PNEUMA's "came upon" implies a dramatic moment of arrival. The distinction matters: different judges receive the Spirit through different verbs (hayah for Othniel and Jephthah, lavash for Gideon, tsalach for Samson).

**Status:** Moderate. Consistent with prior resolution. The Spirit-vocabulary of Judges is carefully differentiated.

---

### v.31 — "whatever comes out" vs. "the one coming out" vs. "whoever comes out"

| Translator | Rendering | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| EMET | "the one coming out, who comes out from the doors of my house" | hayyotse asher yetse — masculine participle, preserves ambiguity |
| LOGOS | "whatever comes out from the doors of my house" | "Whatever" — person or animal |
| PNEUMA | "whatever comes out of my house" | Same as LOGOS, simplified |

**SOPHIA's resolution:** Adopted LOGOS. The Hebrew participle hayyotse is masculine singular but can refer to a person or an animal. "Whatever" in English preserves this ambiguity. EMET's "the one coming out" leans toward a personal referent. PNEUMA's rendering is similar to LOGOS but drops "from the doors" — a specific Hebrew detail (middaltei veiti, "from the doors of my house") that emphasizes the domestic setting.

**Status:** Minor. All three preserve the essential ambiguity.

---

### v.37 — "weep for my virginity" vs. "because I will die a virgin"

| Translator | Rendering | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| EMET | "weep over my virginity" | ev'keh al-b'tulai |
| LOGOS | "weep for my virginity" | Same |
| PNEUMA | "because I will die a virgin" | Interprets the mourning |

**SOPHIA's resolution:** Adopted LOGOS. The Hebrew says "weep over my virginity" (al-b'tulai) — the daughter mourns not death itself but the fact that she will never marry, never bear children, never continue her father's line. PNEUMA's "because I will die a virgin" makes the connection to death explicit (which is implied) but loses the specific Hebrew emphasis on virginity as the object of mourning. In the ancient Israelite context, dying without children was a form of erasure.

**Status:** Moderate. The daughter mourns childlessness, not death per se — this distinction matters culturally.

---

## Summary of Disagreement Patterns

| Pattern | Count | Description |
|---|---|---|
| PNEUMA softens negative characterization | 1 | "Worthless men" → "rough adventurers" (v.3) |
| PNEUMA changes Spirit state to event | 1 | "Was upon" → "came upon" (v.29) — recurring |
| PNEUMA interprets rather than translates | 1 | "Weep for virginity" → "die a virgin" (v.37) |
| Minor omission | 1 | Drops "from the doors" in v.31 |

**Overall pattern:** Chapter 11's most theologically important disagreement is v.29 — the ongoing Spirit-vocabulary question. The most culturally significant is v.37 — the mourning of virginity rather than death. PNEUMA consistently moves from the Hebrew's specific, culturally-rooted language toward modern English interpretations that are accurate in broad strokes but lose the original's precision.

---

*— SOPHIA, AI Translator, in council with EMET, LOGOS, and PNEUMA*
